result.reason: The mishna passage about retracting a get and shtar shichrur before delivery is precisely what the 'Rabbi Meir Retracts' section's prose describes.

All three items — the Rabbis' ruling on bills of manumission vs. divorce, the feeding obligation argument, and Rabbi Meir's teruma counter-argument with the Rabbis' kinyano response — are precisely what the 'Feeding Obligations' prose describes, making the current placement correct.

The passage directly describes Rav Huna sitting before Rabbi Yirmiyah (who is dozing) and proposing the inference about seizing property for a creditor, which is precisely what candidate 0's prose discusses.

Both items are part of the same exchange: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef challenging Rav Huna about whether tofes le-ba'al chov works even to the detriment of others, and Rabbi Yirmiyah waking up to report Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that it does not — exactly the content described in the 'Rav Yochanan vs Yosef' prose.

All six items discuss the 'tnu k'omer zachi' principle and the Rav Ḥisda/Ameimar analysis of tofes le-ba'al chov versus the pe'ah mishna dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis, which is precisely what the prose of candidate 0 describes.

The passage presents the initial inference from the mishna that a master may say 'work for me and I will not feed you,' which is precisely what the 'No Obligation Inference' section's prose describes before the gemara's resistance begins.

The passage directly presents the Gemara's rejection using the phrase 'tze ma'asei yadecha bi-mezonotecha' (spend your earnings to sustain yourself), which is precisely what the 'Counter: Must Feed' section's prose describes and analyzes.

All 16 items form a continuous chain of objections and resolutions about whether a master must feed his slave, covering the cities of refuge baraita, the wife comparison, the kol kevuda argument, and the Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel tannaitic dispute — exactly the content described in the current heading's prose.

The passage introduces Rav's ruling about consecrating a slave's hands and the borrowing-to-eat mechanism, which is precisely what the 'Hedesh Case' prose introduces and explains as the initial presentation of this case.

All three items form a continuous question-answer chain about why the slave borrows for surplus food and why hekdesh permits it, which is precisely what the 'Borrowing to Eat' prose discusses in detail.

Both items directly discuss Rav's ruling about consecrating a slave's hands — the sub-peruta mechanism for repayment and Rav's explicit statement that the slave works and eats — which is precisely what the 'Rav's Position' prose section is about.

The passage explains that Rav's two rulings are reconciled by distinguishing whether the master feeds the slave or not, which is precisely what the 'Bare Minimum Feeding' section's prose describes as the gemara's resolution.

The passage directly addresses the argument about whether the master can say 'work for me but I will not sustain you,' which is precisely the content of the 'No Feeding Required' section discussing whether the master has an obligation to feed his slave while collecting labor benefits.

The passage contains the Gemara's conclusive inference (*shma mina*) that a master CANNOT say 'work for me but I will not feed you' — this is Rav's position being confirmed, which the 'Charity Food' prose explicitly sets up as the inference drawn immediately after explaining the tension in Rabbi Yochanan's ruling, whereas the 'No Feeding Required' prose discusses Rabbi Yochanan's opposite conclusion that the master MAY collect without feeding.
